preceding_messages.speaker: X
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the pairing-supersession, the eight-week counter reset, the "RELOCATION RESET — COMPARISON PAIRING SUPERSEDED" annotation, and the "OBSOLETE BY RELOCATION" retirement marking verbatim; they give the queued re-estimation a defined structural exit rather than an open-ended timeout. For the physical gap in which the relocating site's instruments are idle and the neighborhood-internal coherence statistics are computed over the remaining sites, I mandate that any inter-site spread or directional-spread exceedance during the gap is suppressed for the relocating site's row under a bold "RELOCATION IN PROGRESS — INTER-SITE AUDIT SUPPRESSED" annotation until the new-site instruments pass their first monthly NIST cross-check. The failure this closes: Site 3's two-metre northward shift removes its intermediate-elevation smoothing from the inter-site pressure computation, and the remaining five sites' spread—which sat at 0.44 hPa with all six sites included—widens to 0.57 hPa during the three-day physical gap, tripping the elevation-recording audit a second time before the new-site instruments are even mounted; the audit crew arrives to find the old elevation survey structurally obsolete and the new-site calibration window not yet open, adding two weeks to an already-delayed installation and printing a second DUAL-FLAG week that a year-two appendix reader interprets as repeated institutional confusion. I therefore define the suppression interval as the span between the last valid reading under the old-site serial number and the first valid reading under the new-site serial number, during which all inter-site audit triggers for that row are queued but not executed, and any queued trigger whose exceedance persists beyond the new-site's first monthly cross-check re-enters the formal review queue under standard rules rather than being silently discarded.

preceding_messages.speaker: Y
preceding_messages.text: I adopt the suppression-interval definition, the queued-but-not-executed trigger rule, and the persistence-beyond-cross-check re-entry provision verbatim; they give the relocation gap a defined audit boundary rather than an open-ended timeout. The interval as worded, however, is keyed to instrument serial numbers, but a physical relocation preserves the serial on the moved hardware, so "last valid reading under the old-site serial" and "first valid reading under the new-site serial" resolve to the same serial and the span collapses to zero, leaving the suppression inoperative for the very gap it was designed to cover. I therefore mandate that the suppression interval be re-keyed to the site's surveyed GPS triple—(latitude, longitude, elevation) at ±0.5 m resolution—so that the span runs from the last reading taken at the old triple to the first reading taken at the new triple, with the instrument serial logged alongside for hardware traceability but excluded as an interval boundary. The concrete failure this closes: Site 3's thermistor (serial T-0347) logs its final old-coordinate reading at 18:00 Tuesday, the crew carries it two metres north, and it logs its first new-coordinate reading at 06:00 Thursday; under the serial-keyed definition both boundaries resolve to T-0347 and the suppression interval is zero-length, so Wednesday's inter-site spread—elevated to 0.57 hPa by the temporary loss of Site 3's intermediate-elevation smoothing—executes an immediate elevation-recording audit dispatch to verify a survey already retired by Tuesday's relocation order, printing a confusing duplicate entry in the appendix that a year-two resident reads as procedural incoherence.

target.speaker: X
target.text: I adopt the GPS-triple re-keying and the exclusion of serial number as an interval boundary verbatim; they give the suppression span a physical referent that survives the hardware being carried two metres north. Because a ±0.5 m GPS report in a dense neighborhood is subject to multipath jitter of two to three metres that can converge on the same lobe at similar times of day, I mandate that each coordinate survey—old and new—be fixed by a second method: a transect measurement from the site's commissioning-day reference peg (a stainless-steel dowel driven to bedrock, marked in the horizon-sketch appendix) to the instrument mounting point, recorded to ±2 cm, and that the suppression-interval boundary is defined by the transect offset rather than by the raw GPS report. The failure this closes: at 18:00 Tuesday the crew's handheld receiver resolves under clear western sky to old-coordinate +2 m east, while at 06:00 Thursday it resolves under dawn multipath from a glass office façade to new-coordinate −1 m north, and the reported triples differ by only 0.4 m—inside the ±0.5 m resolution threshold—so the interval collapses to zero and Wednesday's 0.57 hPa spread executes an immediate audit dispatch against a survey already retired by Tuesday's relocation order, printing the same confusing duplicate appendix entry your example describes. I therefore require that any week in which the transect-measured offset and the raw GPS delta disagree by more than 1.5 m triggers a survey-quality annotation "TRIPLES DISCORDANT — INTERVAL DEFINED BY TRANSECT" in the suppression note, so the interval's physical extent is always anchored to the peg geometry and the GPS report serves only as corroborating metadata in the appendix rather than as the operative boundary.
